adults.title: What the Photograph Showed
adults.big_idea: Jesus Christ carries our burdens, often in ways we do not see, and He rescues us not by shortening our course but by helping us lengthen our stride.
adults.objective: Learners will be able to name one way the Savior has carried or strengthened them that they did not see at the time, and will choose one way to turn to Him in a burden they carry now.
prepare: Read Elder Dunn's talk, The Ninety and Ten. Mark the race story (the 1998 ultramarathon through the photograph) and the paragraph that begins “As I marveled at his benevolence”.
Study Isaiah 53:4, Hebrews 12:1 and Doctrine and Covenants 84:88.
Bring a slip of paper and a pen for each person.
Write on the board, and keep covered until segment 4: Shorten my course / Lengthen my stride.
Pray by name for class members who may be at a hard place right now.

segments.name: Where is your mile 90?
steps: Begin with prayer. If you wish, sing one verse of I Need Thee Every Hour.
Explain in two sentences: Elder Michael A. Dunn of the Seventy told of running a 100-mile race. At mile 90, with only 10 miles left, he sat down in the shade of a tree and said, “I give up.”

Read aloud the question he asked at the start of his talk: the Savior promises to carry our burdens, “But what does that look like in practical terms—especially when we are weighed down and seemingly without hope?”
Ask the first question below and give 30 seconds of silence. No one needs to answer aloud. Then invite two or three people to answer the second question.
questions: Where in your life are you at or near a mile 90 right now?
Without sharing private details, what does it feel like to be almost finished and completely out of strength?

segments.name: The race
steps: Tell or read the story, passing the talk from reader to reader, from Ted's promise before the race to the finish line. Stop before the photograph.

Keep these details: Ted had finished this race many times and knew every twist of the trail. He promised to run the second half with Brother Dunn. At mile 90 he knelt, looked him in the eye and said, “I know you can do this, Mike, and I’m going to get you there.” About a hundred yards from the end he stepped aside and said, “This is your race to finish.”
Ask the questions below. Write short answers on the board (for example: he believed, he came, he knew the trail, he stayed, he let him finish).
questions: What did Ted give his friend before he carried anything at all?
Why did it matter that Ted had already run this trail himself?

segments.name: The photograph
steps: Read what the photograph revealed: Ted was carrying two of Elder Dunn's water bottles and his pack, and had carried them every step of the last 10 miles. Elder Dunn never noticed.
Read the line: “Without fanfare or fuss, he simply shouldered my heaviest burden.”
Invite learners to turn to a neighbor and answer the first question below. After two minutes, invite one or two to share with the class.
questions: When have you learned only later that someone had quietly been carrying part of your load?
What changed in you when you found out?

segments.name: Shorter course or longer stride?
steps: Have someone read Isaiah 53:4. Point out that Elder Dunn quoted this verse and said he once assumed it meant the trails we travel would become easier.
Uncover the board. Read the first key quote together: “the Redeemer rescues not by shortening our course but by helping us lengthen our stride.”

Divide into small groups of three or four. Give half the groups Hebrews 12:1 with the last paragraph of the talk, and the other half Doctrine and Covenants 84:88 with the paragraph that begins “Anytime we turn to Christ, we turn a corner.” Ask each group to find one way the Savior lengthens our stride and one experience from their own lives that shows it.
Bring the class together. Take one finding from each group and write it under Lengthen my stride.
Read Elder Chigbundu's sentence from this conference (in the aligned quotes) as a second witness, and ask the last question below.
questions: What is the difference between a prayer to shorten the course and a prayer to lengthen my stride?
Elder Dunn said grace can free us from freight we would otherwise carry. What weight has the Savior taken from you, even while the road stayed long?
Why can we trust the One who, in Elder Dunn's words, knows both the road and us?

segments.name: When we cannot see His hand
steps: Say gently that some in the room may have asked and are still waiting. Read Elder Dunn's promise and what follows it: “I promise that as you expend even your last drops of energy to ask, His helping hand will ultimately give you that much-needed leg up.” Then read the third key quote, on feeling broken.
Read the words of President Dieter F. Uchtdorf that Elder Dunn quoted (in the aligned quotes).
Hand out the slips of paper. Ask everyone to write silently for two minutes: Think of a valley that is now behind you. Looking back, where do you see the Lord's hand, or a Ted He sent?
Invite one person who feels comfortable to share a sentence of what they wrote.
questions: Looking back on a past trial, where do you now see help you could not see then?

segments.name: Choose and act
steps: Explain that Elder Dunn gave a promise rather than an assignment. Invite each person to decide what they will do because of it, and to write one choice on the back of the slip. Offer the ideas in the Act list.
Read the last key quote: “Peace will come even when hoped-for outcomes do not.” Bear your own brief testimony that the Savior knows the road and knows them.
Tell the class you will begin next week by asking who saw unseen help or was sent to be a Ted. Next week, ask it and let two people answer before you start.

key_quotes.text: In other words, the Redeemer rescues not by shortening our course but by helping us lengthen our stride.
I promise that as you expend even your last drops of energy to ask, His helping hand will ultimately give you that much-needed leg up.
take solace knowing that feeling broken does not mean you’ve been abandoned by God.
don’t confuse the perceived invisibility of the Lord’s hand with the inveterate nature of the Lord’s heart. Peace will come even when hoped-for outcomes do not.

scriptures.use: Read aloud at the start of segment 4. Elder Dunn quoted it; ask what he first assumed it meant and what he learned instead.
Half the small groups read it with the last paragraph of the talk and look for what we lay aside and how we are asked to run.
The other groups read it with the paragraph on turning to Christ and look for where the Lord says He and His angels will be.

aligned_quotes.speaker: President Dieter F. Uchtdorf
aligned_quotes.text: Often the deep valleys of our present will be understood only by looking back on them from the mountains of our future experience. Often we can’t see the Lord’s hand in our lives until long after the trials have passed.

aligned_quotes.speaker: Elder Chigbundu
aligned_quotes.text: The burden we carry may not always be removed, but our backs will be built to carry the load placed upon them

takeaways: The Savior often carries what I do not see Him carrying.
He may not shorten my course, but He will lengthen my stride.
Feeling broken does not mean I have been abandoned by God.
act: Each morning this week, pray about one specific burden and ask for strength for that day's stretch of the road, then watch for it.
Before bed, write one line about help you noticed that day, seen or nearly unseen.
Thank a Ted: write or call someone who once carried part of your load and tell them what it meant.
Ask Heavenly Father who near you is at mile 90, and quietly lift one thing for them without fanfare.
music: Where Can I Turn for Peace?
adapt: At home or with a few adults: skip the small groups. Read Hebrews 12:1 together and let each person answer the stride question in turn.
Large class: do segments 3 and 4 in pairs with the people sitting nearby, and take only three or four comments from the whole room.
Short on time: shorten the retelling of the race to two minutes, but keep the photograph and the silent writing.

youth.title: Mile 90
youth.big_idea: When we turn to Jesus Christ, He gives us strength to keep going and often carries more of our load than we can see.
youth.objective: Youth will be able to explain in their own words how the Savior helps by lengthening our stride, and will choose one hard thing to pray about and one person to help this week.
prepare: Read Elder Dunn's talk, The Ninety and Ten, and be ready to tell the race story in about two minutes.
Bring a hymnbook or other book of the same size for every two youth, and a timer (a phone works).
Bring a small card or slip of paper and a pen for each person.
Write on the board: Shorten my course / Lengthen my stride.
Ask the youth to have their scriptures or the Gospel Library app open.

segments.name: The arm challenge
steps: After the prayer, start right away. Put the youth in pairs. One in each pair stands and holds a hymnbook straight out to the side at shoulder height. Start the timer. Anyone whose arm drops sits down. Stop at 60 seconds or when most have dropped.
Round two: same person, same book, but this time the partner rests two fingers under the holder's wrist. Time it again and stop at 60 seconds.
Ask the questions below. Draw out that the book weighed the same and the holder still had to hold it, but quiet help changed what was possible. Tell them today's talk is about that.
questions: What changed between round one and round two?
Holders, did the book get lighter, or did you get help?

segments.name: The race and the photo
steps: Tell the story quickly. Elder Michael A. Dunn of the Seventy once let his running partner Ted talk him into a 100-mile race, about four marathons back to back. Ted had finished it many times and promised to run the second half with him.

Have a youth read what happened at mile 90: he collapsed under a tree and said, “I give up.” Have another read Ted's answer: “I know you can do this, Mike, and I’m going to get you there.” They finished the last 10 miles together, and near the end Ted stepped aside and said, “This is your race to finish.”
Stop. Tell them a photograph of that moment arrived a week or so later and showed a secret. Give pairs 30 seconds to guess what it showed, and take three guesses.

Reveal it: Ted was carrying two of Elder Dunn's water bottles and his pack. He had strapped the pack to his own waist at mile 90 and carried it for the whole last 10 miles, and Elder Dunn never noticed.
questions: Why do you think Ted never mentioned it?
Why did Ted let him cross the finish line on his own?

segments.name: Shorter course or longer stride
steps: Explain that the photo made Elder Dunn think of the Savior. Have everyone find Isaiah 53:4 and one person read it. Elder Dunn said he used to assume this verse meant the trail would get easier.
Read the first key quote together: “the Redeemer rescues not by shortening our course but by helping us lengthen our stride.”

Give the class two minutes to call out real things youth pray for that would shorten the course (cancel the test, make the problem vanish). Write them in the first column. Then, for each one, ask what a longer stride would look like and write that in the second column.

Race: in pairs, look up Doctrine and Covenants 84:88 and Hebrews 12:1. The first pair to find, in each verse, one thing the Lord does and one thing we do stands up and reports. Let a second pair add to it.
Read Elder Chigbundu's sentence from this conference (in the aligned quotes) and ask the last question.
questions: Elder Dunn also said grace can free us from weight we would otherwise carry. How can both be true: He carries, and I still run?
When have you been given strength for something you did not think you could do?

segments.name: What if nothing seems to change?
steps: Say this plainly: sometimes we pray hard and the thing does not go away. Elder Dunn spoke to exactly that. Read his promise in the key quotes, then the next line: “take solace knowing that feeling broken does not mean you’ve been abandoned by God.”
Read the key quote about the Lord's hand and the Lord's heart. Ask a youth to put it in their own words (for example: not seeing His hand does not mean His heart has changed).
Read the words of President Dieter F. Uchtdorf that Elder Dunn quoted (in the aligned quotes).
Pair-share for two minutes on the first question below. Do not press anyone to share something private. Then share a short experience of your own or invite one volunteer.
questions: Think of something hard that is now behind you. Looking back, can you see any help you missed at the time?
What would you say to a friend who feels broken and thinks God has left?

segments.name: Your Ted, and being one
steps: Read: “Other times He simply sends us a Ted.” Hand out the cards.

Silent writing, two minutes. Side one: the name of someone who has been a Ted to you, and what they carried. Side two: the first name or initials of someone you know who might be at mile 90, and one quiet thing you could carry for them.
If phones are allowed, give 60 seconds to send a short thank-you message to the person on side one. If not, they can do it after class.

segments.name: The week's challenge
steps: Give the challenge in the Act list: one hard thing, one prayer a day for stride, one quiet act for the person on the card. Have them write their one hard thing on the card and keep it in their scriptures or phone case.
Point to Elder Dunn's promise once more and bear a brief testimony that the Savior knows the road and knows them.
Tell them you will ask next week for one-sentence reports: where did you get strength, and whose load did you lift? Open next week's class with that question.

key_quotes.text: In other words, the Redeemer rescues not by shortening our course but by helping us lengthen our stride.
I promise that as you expend even your last drops of energy to ask, His helping hand will ultimately give you that much-needed leg up.
don’t confuse the perceived invisibility of the Lord’s hand with the inveterate nature of the Lord’s heart. Peace will come even when hoped-for outcomes do not.
He not only knows the road; He knows you and what you, as noble offspring of the divine, are capable of.

scriptures.use: Everyone finds it and one person reads it before the two-column activity. Elder Dunn quoted it; ask what he first assumed it meant.
Look-up race in pairs: find one thing the Lord promises to do and where He says He will be.
Look-up race in pairs: find what we are to lay aside and how we are to run. Connect it to the last paragraph of the talk.

aligned_quotes.speaker: President Dieter F. Uchtdorf
aligned_quotes.text: Often the deep valleys of our present will be understood only by looking back on them from the mountains of our future experience. Often we can’t see the Lord’s hand in our lives until long after the trials have passed.

aligned_quotes.speaker: Elder Chigbundu
aligned_quotes.text: The burden we carry may not always be removed, but our backs will be built to carry the load placed upon them

takeaways: Jesus Christ knows the road, and He knows me.
He may not make the trail shorter, but He will make me stronger.
Feeling broken does not mean God has left me.
act: Pick one hard thing in your life. Every day this week, pray about it by name and ask for strength for that day, not just for it to go away.
Send a thank-you to someone who has been a Ted to you.
Quietly carry one thing for the person you wrote on your card: sit with them, help with homework, walk with them into class. No fanfare.
Each night, note one moment in your phone or journal when you got through something with more strength than you expected.
adapt: At home: do the arm challenge with a parent and child as partners, tell the story, then let each person fill in a card and share side one aloud.
Large class: run the arm challenge with six volunteers at the front while everyone else times and cheers, and do the two columns in groups of four.
Short on time: keep the arm challenge, the photo reveal, the stride quote and the cards. Shorten the look-up race to Hebrews 12:1 only.

children.title: Jesus Helps Me Keep Going
children.big_idea: Jesus Christ helps me keep going when things are hard.
children.objective: Children will be able to say that Jesus helps them keep going, and will choose to pray when something is hard and to help one person this week.
prepare: Read the race story in Elder Dunn's talk so you can tell it in simple words.
Bring a small backpack or bag with three or four books in it (heavy enough to notice, light enough for a small child), a blanket, a soft ball, paper and crayons.
Bring a picture of Jesus Christ.
Lay a strip of paper or a jump rope on the floor at one side of the room for a finish line.
Write on the board or a paper: Jesus helps me keep going.

segments.name: Sing and say
steps: Sing one verse of I Feel My Savior's Love and invite a child to pray.
Show the picture of Jesus. Teach today's truth with actions: Jesus (point to the picture) helps me (lift both hands up) keep going (march in place).
Say it together three times: slowly, quickly, then in a whisper.

segments.name: The long, long race
steps: Tell the children that Elder Dunn, a leader in the Church, once ran a very, very long race. It lasted all day, all night, and into the next morning. Have everyone stand and run in place.

Say: He ran in the hot afternoon (wipe your forehead). He ran in the dark (hands over eyes, peek out). His friend Ted came to run with him (wave to a friend). He got slower and slower (run in slow motion).
Hold the blanket up like a shady tree and have the children sit down under it. Say: He was so tired that he sat down under a tree. He was almost done, but he said, “I give up.”
Kneel down as Ted did. Say: Ted knelt down, looked at him and said he knew he could do it and would get him there. Ask the first question below.
Have the children get up as Elder Dunn did: first walk, then hobble, then shuffle to the finish line on the floor. Cheer quietly when everyone has crossed.
questions: How do you think he felt when his friend said that?
What helped him get up again?

segments.name: The secret in the picture
steps: Sit in a circle. Let each child lift the backpack for a moment. Ask one child to carry it across the room and back.
Ask the same child to walk across again. This time, walk beside the child and hold the backpack up by its top handle so it feels light. Ask the first question below.

Tell the secret: After the race, someone sent Elder Dunn a picture. In the picture he saw something he had not noticed. Ted had been carrying his pack and two of his water bottles the whole last part of the race. Ted never said a word about it.

Hold up the picture of Jesus. Say: When Elder Dunn saw that picture, he thought about Jesus. Jesus is our best helper. He helps us even when we do not see Him. Say the truth together with the actions.
questions: What felt different the second time?
Who helps us even when we cannot see Him?

segments.name: When it is hard, I can pray
steps: Tell the children that Elder Dunn said silent prayers all through the race. A silent prayer is one we say to Heavenly Father in our hearts.

Open your scriptures to Psalm 55:22 and read it aloud, or let an older child read it. Ask what the verse says we can do with something heavy. Explain in simple words: we can give our heavy things to the Lord, and He will help us.

Play a ball game. Sit in a circle. Roll the ball to a child and name something hard (learning something new, feeling scared at night, feeling sad, being left out, a long chore). The child folds their arms and says: I can pray. Everyone answers with the actions: Jesus helps me keep going. The child rolls the ball back.
Give every child a turn. Let older children name the hard thing for the next child.
questions: When could you say a silent prayer in your heart?

segments.name: Draw the trail
steps: Give each child paper and crayons. Ask them to draw a long path across the paper, then draw themselves on the path doing something that is hard for them.
Ask them to add a helper on the path: Jesus beside them, or someone Heavenly Father sent to help, like a parent, a teacher or a friend.
Walk around and ask each child to tell you about the picture. Help them write or say today's truth: Jesus helps me keep going.
Invite two or three children to show their pictures to the class.
questions: Who is helping you in your picture?

segments.name: I can be a helper like Ted
steps: Say: Elder Dunn taught that sometimes Heavenly Father sends us a helper like Ted. We can be that helper for someone else.

Act it out. One child pretends to be tired and sits down. Another child kneels beside them and says kind words, such as: I know you can do this. I will help you. Then they walk to the finish line together. Trade places and repeat with new children.
Ask the question below and take several answers.
questions: What is one kind thing you could do this week for someone who is having a hard time?

segments.name: Choose and close
steps: Say the truth one more time with the actions. Tell the children in a sentence that you know Jesus loves them and will help them.
Invite them to do two things this week: pray when something is hard, and help one person the way Ted did. Ask each child to whisper to a neighbor who they might help.
Send the drawings home. Next week, begin by asking: When did Jesus help you keep going? Who did you help?

key_quotes.text: I know you can do this, Mike, and I’m going to get you there.
Anytime we turn to Christ, we turn a corner.
Other times He simply sends us a Ted.

scriptures.use: Read aloud in the prayer segment (an older child may read). Ask what the verse says we can do with something heavy.
For older children: read it aloud after the race story and ask what Jesus said is possible with God. Connect it to Elder Dunn finishing the race.

aligned_quotes.speaker: Elder Kearon
aligned_quotes.text: Our Saviour constantly sought out the most desperate souls sinking into darkness and dread and lifted them up. And He wants to lift you!

takeaways: When something is hard, I can pray.
I can be a helper like Ted.
act: When something feels hard this week, stop and say a prayer, out loud or in your heart.
Help one person the way Ted did: carry something, sit by someone, or say kind words.
Show your drawing to your family and tell them the story of the long race.
music: If the Savior Stood Beside Me

adapt.younger: For ages 3–7: keep the story to a few sentences and let the acting do the teaching. Run, sit under the blanket tree and shuffle to the finish line twice if they enjoy it. In the ball game, you name every hard thing and say the answer with them. Skip the role play and simply ask each child to show you helping hands. Repeat the truth with actions after every activity.
adapt.older: For ages 8–11: let a child read Psalm 55:22 and another read Matthew 19:26. Read them Elder Kearon's words in the aligned quotes and ask whom Jesus wants to lift. Ask a harder question: Jesus did not make Elder Dunn's race shorter, so how did He help? Let older children play Ted in the story, lead the ball game and help younger children with their drawings.
